q: Ethyl propanoate is treated with one equivalent of NaOEt in ethanol, and the mixture is then acidified. What is the Claisen condensation product?
h: The α-carbon (C2) of one ester attacks the C=O of a second ester, and ethoxide leaves. Which carbon of the product carries the CH<sub>3</sub> branch?
w: The enolate of one ester (nucleophilic C2, which carries a CH3) attacks the carbonyl of a second ester; the tetrahedral intermediate expels EtO−, giving a β-keto ester. The CH3 stays on the carbon between the two C=O groups: ethyl 2-methyl-3-oxopentanoate, C8H14O3 = 2 C5H10O2 − C2H5OH.
x: This product lacks the CH<sub>3</sub> branch (C<sub>7</sub>); it would come from ethyl acetate plus ethyl propanoate. The nucleophilic carbon of ethyl propanoate is the CH<sub>2</sub>, so it keeps its CH<sub>3</sub>.
This is an aldol-type alcohol. In a Claisen the tetrahedral intermediate is not protonated; it expels ethoxide, regenerating a C=O (a ketone).
Losing both ethoxy groups gives a β-diketone; only one ester undergoes acyl substitution, so the product keeps one OEt.

q: Which ester gives little or no Claisen condensation product when treated with NaOEt in ethanol?
h: The Claisen equilibrium is driven to completion by one last step after the β-keto ester forms. What does that step require of the product?
w: The Claisen addition–elimination steps are uphill. The reaction is pulled forward because ethoxide removes the very acidic H between the two C=O groups of the β-keto ester (pKa ≈ 11). Ethyl 2-methylpropanoate has only one α-H; after condensation the central carbon carries two CH3 groups and no H, so this driving deprotonation is impossible and the equilibrium returns to starting ester.
x: Ethyl acetate has three α-H's; its product, ethyl acetoacetate, has an acidic CH<sub>2</sub> between the carbonyls that ethoxide deprotonates.
Ethyl propanoate has two α-H's; its β-keto ester product still has one H between the carbonyls to drive the reaction.
Ethyl phenylacetate has two benzylic α-H's; its product keeps an acidic H between the carbonyls and condenses well.

q: Diethyl heptanedioate is treated with NaOEt in ethanol and then with dilute acid. What is the product?
h: A Dieckmann reaction is an intramolecular Claisen. Count the atoms from the enolate α-carbon to the other C=O carbon, inclusive.
w: Number the diacid chain C1–C7 (C1 and C7 are the ester carbons). The enolate at C2 attacks C7; the ring contains C2, C3, C4, C5, C6 and C7: a six-membered ring. Loss of ethoxide gives ethyl 2-oxocyclohexane-1-carboxylate, C9H14O3 (diester minus EtOH).
x: A five-membered Dieckmann product comes from diethyl hexanedioate (adipate), which has one fewer CH<sub>2</sub>.
A seven-membered product would require diethyl octanedioate; heptanedioate gives a six-membered ring.
Cyclohexanone forms only after ester hydrolysis and decarboxylation with heat; dilute acid workup at room temperature leaves the β-keto ester intact.

q: What is the final product of this sequence?
h: Step 1 is a Dieckmann cyclization (count the ring size). Where is the most acidic H in the product, and what happens to a β-keto acid on heating?
w: Diethyl hexanedioate (adipate) undergoes Dieckmann cyclization to ethyl 2-oxocyclopentane-1-carboxylate, whose enolate (between the two C=O groups) is methylated by CH3I at that carbon. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the ester to a β-keto acid, which decarboxylates. The product is 2-methylcyclopentanone.
x: Adipate (six-carbon diacid) gives a five-membered ring; a six-membered ring needs heptanedioate.
This omits the methylation. The doubly stabilized enolate is alkylated by CH<sub>3</sub>I before hydrolysis, and the methyl survives decarboxylation.
β-Keto acids lose CO<sub>2</sub> on heating through a cyclic transition state; the carboxylic acid does not survive step 3.

q: Acetone is added slowly to a mixture of NaH and excess ethyl benzoate; the mixture is then acidified. What is the major product?
h: Only one partner can form an enolate. Which C=O is the electrophile, and what leaves from it?
w: Ethyl benzoate has no α-H, so it can only be the electrophile. The acetone enolate attacks the ester carbonyl, ethoxide is expelled, and the β-diketone is deprotonated (driving the reaction) until acid workup. The product of this crossed Claisen is 1-phenylbutane-1,3-dione.
x: Ethyl 3-oxo-3-phenylpropanoate would need an ester enolate (from ethyl acetate). Here the enolate comes from acetone, so the product keeps a methyl ketone, not an ester.
Mesityl oxide is acetone's self-aldol condensation product. Slow addition of acetone into excess, more reactive ethyl benzoate makes the crossed Claisen dominant.
This 1,3-diketone has two benzoyl groups; it would need acetophenone as the enolate partner, and no acetophenone is present.

q: In a crossed Claisen condensation with ethyl acetate, the second ester should be able to act only as the electrophile. Which ester is not suitable for this role?
h: Look for α-hydrogens on each ester.
w: A partner that acts only as an acceptor must lack α-H's. Ethyl phenylacetate (PhCH2CO2Et) has two acidic benzylic α-H's, so it would also form an enolate and give a mixture of self- and crossed-Claisen products.
x: Ethyl benzoate has no α-carbon bearing H (the carbonyl is attached to the ring), so it can only be attacked.
Diethyl carbonate, (EtO)<sub>2</sub>C=O, has no α-carbon at all; it is a standard acylating partner that installs a CO<sub>2</sub>Et group.
Ethyl formate, HCO<sub>2</sub>Et, has no α-carbon; it installs a CHO (formyl) group.

q: Which alkyl halide(s), used in a malonic ester synthesis, give 2-methylbutanoic acid?
c: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br and CH<sub>3</sub>I (one after the other)
h: In the product, find the α-carbon (next to CO<sub>2</sub>H). It was the malonate CH<sub>2</sub>. What groups were added to it?
w: Malonic ester synthesis gives R(R′)CH–CO2H: the malonate CH2 becomes the α-carbon, and one CO2Et becomes the CO2H while the other is lost as CO2. The α-carbon of 2-methylbutanoic acid carries an ethyl and a methyl, so alkylate with CH3CH2Br and then CH3I (either order).
x: A propyl group plus a methyl gives 2-methylpentanoic acid, one carbon too many.
A sec-butyl group on the malonate carbon gives 3-methylpentanoic acid; the branch ends up at C3, not C2 (and secondary halides alkylate poorly).
A single ethyl gives butanoic acid; the methyl branch on C2 needs a second alkylation.

q: Diethyl malonate is treated with two equivalents of NaOEt and one equivalent of 1,4-dibromobutane, then heated with aqueous acid. What is the final product?
h: The first alkylation attaches the four-carbon chain; the second enolate is formed on the same carbon and displaces the other Br intramolecularly. Count the ring atoms.
w: The malonate carbon is alkylated by one end of the dibromide; a second deprotonation at the same carbon lets it displace the other bromide intramolecularly. The ring contains the malonate carbon plus four CH2 groups: a five-membered ring. Hydrolysis and decarboxylation of the 1,1-diacid give cyclopentanecarboxylic acid.
x: A six-membered ring would need 1,5-dibromopentane. The ring holds the four chain carbons plus the malonate carbon.
A four-membered ring would come from 1,3-dibromopropane.
A 1,1-dicarboxylic acid (a malonic acid) loses CO<sub>2</sub> on heating, so only one CO<sub>2</sub>H remains.

q: What is the final product of this acetoacetic ester synthesis?
h: The acetoacetic ester synthesis turns R–X into a methyl ketone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>–R. What happens to the ester group in hot aqueous acid?
w: The enolate (from the CH2 between the two C=O groups) is benzylated by SN2. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the ester to a β-keto acid, which decarboxylates. The CO2Et carbon is lost, leaving CH3C(=O)CH2–CH2Ph: 4-phenylbutan-2-one.
x: This is one carbon short: the original CH<sub>2</sub> of the acetoacetate stays in the product between the C=O and the new benzyl group.
A carboxylic acid product is the outcome of a malonic ester synthesis. Acetoacetic ester loses the ester carbon and keeps the ketone.
This is the alkylated β-keto ester before step 3. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes and decarboxylates it.

q: Which alkyl halides should be used, in two separate alkylation steps, to make 3-methylhexan-2-one by the acetoacetic ester synthesis?
h: Keep the CH<sub>3</sub>C(=O) unit and the α-carbon from ethyl acetoacetate. Which groups are attached to that α-carbon in the target?
w: In the target, CH3C(=O)– comes from the acetoacetate, and C3 is the original active CH2. C3 carries a methyl and an n-propyl group, so the ester is alkylated with CH3I and CH3CH2CH2Br (in either order) before hydrolysis and decarboxylation.
x: A single butyl group gives heptan-2-one, a straight-chain ketone with no branch at C3.
Methyl plus ethyl gives 3-methylpentan-2-one, one carbon short.

A secondary halide attaches through its C2, giving CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (4-methylheptan-2-one), and secondary halides alkylate enolates poorly.

q: Which carboxylic acid cannot be prepared efficiently by a malonic ester synthesis?
h: Work backward to the halide(s) needed for each acid. Each alkylation is an S<sub>N</sub>2 step.
w: A malonic ester synthesis gives RCH2CO2H or RR′CHCO2H, where each R comes from an SN2 alkylation. 3,3-Dimethylbutanoic acid, (CH3)3C–CH2CO2H, needs R = tert-butyl, i.e., (CH3)3CBr, a tertiary halide that undergoes E2 with the malonate anion instead of SN2.
x: 3-Phenylpropanoic acid needs benzyl bromide, an excellent S<sub>N</sub>2 substrate.
2-Methylpentanoic acid needs 1-bromopropane and CH<sub>3</sub>I, both good S<sub>N</sub>2 substrates.
Pent-4-enoic acid needs allyl bromide, an activated primary halide that alkylates readily.

q: Which compound loses CO<sub>2</sub> most readily when heated to about 100 °C?
h: Decarboxylation on gentle heating requires a carbonyl positioned to accept electrons through a six-membered cyclic transition state.
w: A β-keto acid decarboxylates easily: the acid H is transferred to the ketone O through a six-membered cyclic transition state as CO2 leaves, giving an enol that tautomerizes to the ketone (acetone here).
x: In a γ-keto acid the ketone is too far away to form the six-membered cyclic transition state.
A β-hydroxy acid has no C=O at the β-position to accept the electrons; it may dehydrate but does not lose CO<sub>2</sub> easily.
Benzoic acid has no β-carbonyl and its carboxyl is attached to an sp<sup>2</sup> ring carbon; it is stable well above 100 °C.

q: 3-Oxobutanoic acid decarboxylates on warming. What is the organic species formed directly in the CO2-loss step, before any tautomerization?
h: In the cyclic transition state, the carboxyl H moves to the ketone oxygen as the C–C bond to CO<sub>2</sub> breaks. Where does the new π bond form?
w: In the six-membered cyclic transition state, the O–H proton moves to the ketone oxygen, the C–CO2 bond breaks, and its electrons form a C=C between the α-carbon and the former carbonyl carbon. The first product is the neutral enol, prop-1-en-2-ol, which then tautomerizes to acetone.
x: Acetone is the final product, but it forms only after the enol tautomerizes; the concerted CO<sub>2</sub>-loss step gives the enol.
Under these neutral thermal conditions the proton is transferred within the cyclic transition state, so no free carbanion (enolate) forms.
Ketene would require losing water or an alcohol from an acid derivative; decarboxylation removes CO<sub>2</sub> and keeps the ketone oxygen.

q: What is the final product of this sequence?
h: A stabilized malonate anion adds 1,4 to an enone. Then count the carbons that remain after one CO<sub>2</sub>H is lost.
w: The malonate anion is a soft, stabilized nucleophile and adds to the β-carbon of methyl vinyl ketone (Michael addition), giving (EtO2C)2CH–CH2CH2C(=O)CH3. Hydrolysis and decarboxylation leave one CO2H on the former malonate carbon: HO2C–CH2–CH2CH2C(=O)CH3, 5-oxohexanoic acid.
x: This comes from 1,2-addition to the C=O. Stabilized enolates such as malonate add reversibly at C=O and end up in the more stable 1,4 (conjugate) adduct.
4-Oxopentanoic acid is one carbon short; the MVK unit contributes four carbons and the malonate CH<sub>2</sub> plus one CO<sub>2</sub>H contribute two.
This is one carbon too long; only two carbons of malonate remain (CH<sub>2</sub> and one CO<sub>2</sub>H), not three.
